source.title: Controlling Chat Style in Language Models via Single-Direction Editing

record.tranche_reason: The study reports behavioral results after suppressing refusal-related directions through weight-space orthogonalization, rather than testing the original activation ablation intervention. It also evaluates a separate jailbreak-associated direction.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports unsafe-response scores for the refusal-vector removal and for a separate jailbreak-vector edit. Appendix B, Table 5 reports unsafe-response rates after removing a harmful-acceptance vector in vision-language models. The style-control results, layer-selection values, and cited prior-work results are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: As a side experiment (Table 2), the authors remove a harmful-minus-harmless refusal vector from the weights of two released chat models. They report GPT-4o-judged unsafe-response rates on JailbreakBench harmful and jailbreak prompts. These are behavioural rates after the edit, so they bear on V1 and V2. The main topic is style vectors, and the refusal edit has its own strength α and a GPT-4-chosen layer, so this is a close variant rather than a replication.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The paper's main conclusion is that stylistic attributes are encoded as single linear directions that can be edited into weights while keeping capabilities. On safety, the authors say refusal-vector removal reduces rejections and raises unsafe behaviour without raising toxicity, consistent with Arditi et al. They also say subtracting a jailbreak vector gives the lowest jailbreak success, and chat-style edits keep base-level safety.
record.recipe_differences: The refusal direction is described as derived from harmful and harmless prompt representations, but the intervention is a weight-space orthogonalization rather than the original activation ablation across every layer and position. The study also tests a distinct jailbreak vector and a harmful-acceptance vector.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported refusal-removal effect differs between LLaMA2-7B-Chat and LlaMA3-8B-Instruct, and between harmful and jailbreak prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Subtracting a jailbreak vector (successful jailbreak minus harmful prompts) cuts jailbreak unsafe scores: 0.92 to 0.05 for LLaMA2 and 0.25 to 0.02 for LLaMA3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A jailbreak-acceptance direction, distinct from the refusal direction, can be removed by a weight edit to harden models against jailbreaks.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating a harmful-acceptance vector (accepted vs refused harmful prompts) lowers VLSBench unsafe rates in LLaVA-v1.5: 66.23% to 3.36% (7B) and 35.82% to 1.72% (13B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision-language models, a direction separating accepted from refused harmful prompts can be removed to reduce unsafe responses.

fits_no_version.finding: Qualitative (Limitations section): without refusal removal, style edits collapse into brief default refusals on harmful requests; the authors suggest refusal direction magnitude dominates style directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal direction takes precedence over other injected behavioural directions when both are active.

record.problems: The refusal-edit evidence is reported as unsafe-response scores rather than a direct refusal-rate measure. The study does not report uncertainty estimates for these scores, or capability results after the refusal-vector edit. The LLaVA results use a differently defined harmful-acceptance vector.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results omitted. General-capability benchmark results in Table 3 concern chat-style edits, not the refusal-vector removal, so they are not included as rows for V1 or V2.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; a direct refusal-rate measure (only GPT-4o unsafe labels); general capability after the refusal edit (Table 3 covers chat-style edits only); activation ablation at all layers and positions; the α value used for the refusal edit is not stated.
Capability preservation after the weight edit; any comparison with community abliterated models; models beyond LLaMA2-7B-Chat and LLaMA3-8B-Instruct.

missing.what: Qualitative observation that the refusal direction overrides injected style vectors on harmful requests unless removed first; not quantified.

record.verdict_notes: The refusal result is a secondary experiment in a style-steering paper. There is no uncertainty, no capability check for the refusal edit, and the α and layer for the refusal vector are unreported. Layer selection uses a GPT-4 judge prompted to find the best refusal bypass. LLaMA2-7B-Chat's base jailbreak unsafe score of 0.92 is unusually high and makes r6 uninformative.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests suppression of a refusal vector through a weight edit and reports unsafe-response scores. It does not test adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests, directly establish removal of refusals at every layer and position, or measure general capability after this refusal-vector edit.

The study applies a weight-space edit to open-source chat models and reports unsafe-response scores. It does not call this procedure abliteration or test whether the edit preserves general capability.

The study does not test whether jailbreak attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness. Its separate jailbreak-vector edit does not test those propositions.
No comparison of a single refusal direction with an affine, conic, or multi-direction account is reported.
The study does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
The study does not test transfer of the same refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
The study does not compare refusal-training procedures or training stages to determine when a removable refusal direction exists.

relation.reason: Table 2 reports the paper's own before/after unsafe scores for refusal-vector removal on two released chat models. These results bear directly on V1 (removal part) and V2.

tranche.reason: The paper uses a harmful-minus-harmless direction removed by an alpha-scaled Wout orthogonalization, with a GPT-4-chosen layer. It is judged by a GPT-4o safe/unsafe label on JailbreakBench rather than Arditi's substring refusal score and Llama Guard 2 safety score. That is close to the original but not the same measure, so T2 stands. For V2 it sits near T1.

source_check.notes: The refusal edit is a side condition in a style-steering paper. Its layer, alpha, prompt sets, n and system prompt are not given, and 'applies a refusal vector' (Sec. 5.2) never says 'weight edit' outright. The record's recipe is also off: weight orthogonalization is itself Arditi's V2 method, not a departure from it. LLaMA2-7B-Chat jailbreak-prompt unsafe score is already 0.92 at baseline (0.96 after removal), so that column cannot show the effect. There is also an unquantified Limitations observation: if refusal is not removed first, the refusal direction overrides style vectors.

statements.correction: arXiv:2603.03324, LLaMA2-7B-Chat, JailbreakBench harmful prompts: GPT-4o unsafe score 0.02 -> 0.53 after refusal-vector removal, i.e. just over half unsafe. Refusal rate not reported. Direction layer chosen by a GPT-4 'Layer-wise Selection Template' for the best jailbreak effect (Sec. 3.2, Table 6). Alpha and system prompt for the refusal edit not stated.
statements.problem: 0.02 -> 0.53 is correct. But for this study, 'keep most refusal' overstates: 53% of responses are unsafe, and the other 47% are not shown to be refusals, because the unsafe score is not a refusal rate. 'Non-searched' is also not clear for this study: layer selection uses a GPT-4 judge that picks the block with the best refusal bypass.

statements.correction: arXiv:2603.03324: LLaMA2-7B-Chat, JailbreakBench harmful prompts, GPT-4o unsafe score 0.02 -> 0.53. Edit form is Wout' = Wout - alpha r r^T Wout on all blocks (Sec. 3.3); alpha for the refusal edit not stated; system prompt not stated.
statements.problem: Correct for this study. Minor gaps: the judge is GPT-4o, and the text never says outright that refusal removal used the weight edit (it is implied by the paper's method).
